The town hired a cartographer to map the places people went when they said they were going nowhere.

It was a small commission, poorly funded. He received a bicycle, a notebook, and permission to ask impolite questions.

At first, nobody helped.

“Nowhere,” said the baker, locking the shop.

“Just out,” said a girl with a fishing rod and no hook.

“Mind your business,” said the mayor, who was carrying two pears.

So the cartographer rode his bicycle through the town and waited.

He found a bench behind the railway station where you could hear every departure but see no trains. He found a strip of grass between the cemetery wall and the hardware store, warm long after sunset. Beneath the bridge, someone had arranged seven flat stones in a circle. Nothing stood in the middle.

He marked these places carefully.

His first draft was rejected.

“These are ordinary locations,” the council said. “We already have a map of those.”

He returned to work.

This time, beside the bench, he wrote: *Where a person may reconsider a journey without buying another ticket.*

Beside the grass: *For sitting after the hardware store has closed, particularly if you have forgotten what you meant to repair.*

Beside the stones, he wrote nothing. But he drew all seven.

Slowly, people began to visit his office.

A woman told him about the third-floor landing of the hospital, where the window opened despite the notice saying it did not.

A boy described an alley where a dog would lean against your legs, provided you made no attempt to pet it.

The mayor came in after dark.

“There’s an orchard outside town,” she said. “Abandoned. I used to go there with my brother.”

“May I put it on the map?”

She considered this.

“Put the orchard on it,” she said. “Leave my brother out.”

By winter, the map was finished. The printer complained about the empty spaces, but the cartographer would not fill them.

Copies appeared in kitchens and railway offices. People penciled in corrections. One bench had been removed. The hospital window had been painted shut. Someone added a shortcut to the orchard, then crossed it out because it led through a field with a bull.

The cartographer kept that copy.

In spring, when the council offered him another commission, he asked for a week to think. He left his bicycle outside the office and walked down to the station.

For once, he took nothing to write with.
